```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from npn_study/scripts/90_npn_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Work in progress
This page is updated as the analysis runs. Results are preliminary and will change.
The study stands on its own (its own data, regions and code); a related project maps
[fuel phenology regions](index.html) from satellite greenness.
:::

## At a glance

**The question.** Curing is the fuel variable fire managers care about most for grasses, and
the U.S. has almost no ground record of it. USA National Phenology Network (NPN) observers
record, for tagged grass plants, what share of the plant is still green, several times a
month. This study asks what that record shows: when grasses green up and cure, where and
for which grass types, how much those dates change from year to year, and whether weather
explains the early and late years.

**Why it matters.** Fire danger systems estimate grass curing from weather indices or
satellite greenness, and both are rarely checked against plants on the ground. This study
starts from the ground dates: it describes when grasses green up and cure across the
country, asks how much of that is fixed by place and how much changes from year to year, and
tests what can be predicted from weather at all. The result is a ground baseline that any
weather- or satellite-based curing estimate can be checked against.

**Questions.**

1. **The record:** how many sites, species, years and plants carry usable curves, and where?
2. **Climatology:** typical green-up, curing and cured dates for cool-season (C3) and
   warm-season (C4) grasses, by region.
3. **Place versus year:** how much of each date is fixed by place, and how much varies from
   year to year? Is the year-to-year part shared among plants and sites?
4. **Climate across space:** do typical dates follow each site's climate?
5. **Weather from year to year:** how far up a ladder of models, from one driver to a random
   forest, does it take to explain a grass's early and late years?
6. **Is simple enough?** Where do simple process rules sit on that ladder?

**What we have found so far (October 2026).**

- **The record is mostly NEON.** 6,331 plant-years of percent-green curves (1,617 plants,
  130 sites, 70 species, 2014–2024). 94 % come from 36 National Ecological Observatory
  Network field sites, where technicians follow five tagged plants per species in natural
  plots; the other 94 sites add spatial coverage but few years each.
- **Typical green-up follows site climate; typical curing much less.** Across sites,
  warm-season grasses green up earlier where spring is warmer and later where more of the
  rain falls in summer, and site climate predicts their typical green-up at a new place
  (about a third of the variation once nearby plots are held out together). Cool-season curing follows the species and the site's
  wetness; warm-season curing dates are not explained by species, region or climate.
- **Place dominates.** Two-thirds to four-fifths of the variation in a grass's dates is
  where it grows and which species it is.
- **No weather model beats the typical date.** From one driver to a random forest, every
  model does as well as or worse than each grass's typical date, for green-up, curing and
  the cured date.
- **There is a shared year signal, mostly missed.** A quarter to two-fifths of the
  year-to-year variation is shared by the grasses at a site (about 18 days), mostly local to
  the site rather than region-wide. Moisture and summer vapour pressure deficit track it in the
  expected direction, but too weakly to predict it.
- **2016 and 2017 look different.** In those two years many NEON plants never reached
  their usual peak greenness, at most sites at once, which points to a change in how
  percent green was judged rather than weather. Leaving them out leaves every conclusion
  unchanged but removes about a third of the shared curing signal.

**Status (October 2026).**

## Data and methods

### Data

- **Ground observations.** USA-NPN status and intensity records for grasses and sedges,
  2014–2024: on each visit the observer records, for a tagged plant, which class of "percent
  of the plant that is green" it is in (< 5, 5–24, 25–49, 50–74, 75–94, ≥ 95 %). 94 % of the
  plant-years come from the 36 NEON field sites, where technicians follow about five tagged
  plants per species; the rest are volunteer and managed sites. A plant-year is usable with at
  least 6 readings and a peak above 50 % green: 6,331 plant-years, 1,617 plants, 130 sites,
  70 species after crops (wheat, corn) are removed.
- **Grass types.** Each species is labelled cool-season (C3) or warm-season (C4), annual or
  perennial, and native or introduced, from the literature (72 species; under review with
  USA-NPN).
- **Climate.** PRISM daily 4 km precipitation, minimum and maximum temperature and maximum
  vapour pressure deficit, 2001–2025, at every site; site normals over 2002–2025.
- **Regions.** EPA / CEC Level II ecoregions (CEC 1997): the 130 sites fall in 17.
- **Fuel attributes.** For each species: whether it is one of the invasive grasses shown to raise
  fire occurrence and frequency across U.S. ecoregions (Fusco et al. 2019), and its mature height
  and growth form from the USDA PLANTS database. For each site: the Scott & Burgan (2005) fire
  behavior fuel model from LANDFIRE (FBFM40, 30 m).

### Methods

- **Dates.** Green-up and curing are the dates a tagged plant passes 50 % green going up and
  coming down; the cured date is when it is fully cured. Crops (wheat, corn) are left out,
  and species are labeled C3 (cool-season) or C4 (warm-season) from the literature. Dates
  more than 90 days from the series' usual date count as a season mismatch and are not used.
- **Two sets of plants.** *The record, the typical dates and climate across space* use
  every plant-year with at least 6 readings and a peak above 50 % green (the NPN-derived
  "usable" curves), and a site and species with even one year: 6,331 plant-years. *The
  year-to-year analyses* need at least 12 readings per plant-year and 3 or more years per
  site and species: 707 series-years in 181 series (86 sites, 67 species), of which 289
  green-up, 529 curing and 461 cured series-years are scored. A series-year is one site,
  species and year, the median over that site-year's plants.
- **Typical date.** For each site and species, the circular median of its plants' dates
  over all years.
- **Regions.** EPA / Commission for Environmental Cooperation Level II ecoregions (CEC 1997),
  assigned to every site by its location; the 130 sites fall in 17 of them.
- **Fuel model at a site.** The LANDFIRE fuel model at the site's point; where that cell is
  nonburnable (a road, building or water) or missing, the most common burnable model within 90 m.
  Fuel models describe the fuel bed, not the species, so they are a site attribute; no fuel rating
  is assigned to a species. PLANTS "fire tolerance" rates how well a plant survives fire, not the
  fuel it makes, and is listed for reference only.
- **Weather.** Daily PRISM at each site, 2001–2025: growing degree-days, seasonal
  temperature, freeze dates, chilling, seasonal rain, vapour pressure deficit, rain events
  and dry spells, monsoon onset, and a moisture memory (a running average of daily
  precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration, over 15, 30 and 60 days). Each is used
  as a departure from the site's own average, so place is removed from both sides.
- **Two sets of curing drivers.** *Lead*: only weather known by the series' typical date
  minus 14 days (spring conditions, rain after the typical green-up, moisture memory and
  heat at that cutoff), the operational case. *Hindcast*: adds the summer and fall windows,
  which can run past the date.
- **The ladder**, the same data, folds and scores at each step:
  - **L0, typical date:** the series' average over the training years. This is the bar.
  - **L1, one driver:** March–April temperature for green-up; moisture memory at the cutoff
    (lead) or June–August rain (hindcast) for curing.
  - **L2, process rule:** green-up when growing degree-days reach the series' usual amount;
    curing when the 30-day moisture memory falls below the series' usual level and stays
    there (within 60 days of the typical date), or at the first hard fall freeze if earlier.
  - **L3, regression:** up to four drivers chosen by forward selection, per C3/C4.
  - **L4, random forest:** all drivers plus site climate, pathway and life cycle.
- **Scoring.** Leave one year out (every series loses the same year at once). Mean absolute
  error in days; skill = 1 − error / error of the typical date; and the correlation of each
  model's predicted departure with the observed one.

| Other NPN sites | 371 | 179 | 94 | 34 | 7,660 | 160 / 200 / 183 |
| Year-to-year set (≥ 12 readings, ≥ 3 years) | 5,668 | 1,417 | 48 | 60 | 195,405 | 2,514 / 4,385 / 3,171 |

```{r fig-npn-sites}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_sites",

  "Map of the contiguous U.S. with NPN grass study sites coloured by cool-season, warm-season or both grass types, sized by plant-years, filled for NEON sites.")
```

```{r fig-npn-regions}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_regions",
  "The EPA Level II ecoregions used to group results throughout this page, with the study sites. Ecoregions are shaded by their Level I family, strongly where the record has sites; the list gives each such ecoregion's sites (NEON in brackets) and plant-years.",
  "Map of EPA Level II ecoregions in the contiguous U.S. with region codes and the study sites, and a list of ecoregions with their site and plant-year counts.")
```

```{r fig-npn-record}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_record",
  "What the record is made of: the percent-green class of each reading, how many readings each plant-year carries, and how often a plant greens up a second time after curing, by region.",
  "Three panels: horizontal bars of reading shares by percent-green class; box summaries of readings per plant-year for NEON, other and managed sites; bars of second green-up share by region.")
```

- **NEON carries the record.** 94 % of plant-years, and 96 % of the readings, come from the
  36 NEON sites. Their plants are read about weekly through most of the year (median 35
  readings per plant-year). The other 94 sites are read just as often while observed, but
  over shorter spans (median 14–16 readings), so they add places, not years: in the
  year-to-year set they are only 16 sites.
- **The whole scale is used.** A third of all readings are in the top class (95 % green or
  more); each of the other classes holds 10–20 %.
- **Second green-ups are common.** 18 % of plant-years fall below 25 % green and then come
  back above 50 % at least three weeks later (cool-season 15 %, warm-season 19 %), most often
  in Mediterranean California (44 %, the annual grasses greening again with the first fall
  rains within the same calendar year), the Mississippi Alluvial and Southeast USA Coastal
  Plains (35 %), the Southeastern USA Plains (27 %) and the Warm Deserts (27 %). In 276 plant-years the 50 % curing date belongs to the second cycle.
- **Some plants never pass 50 % green.** 6 % of NEON plant-years with enough readings stay
  below 50 % all year, so they have no green-up or curing date. Almost all are in 2016 and
  2017 (see [the check below](#a-check-2016-and-2017)).

## The species

```{r fig-npn-species}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_species",
  "Typical season of each species observed at three or more sites: green-up (open circle), 50 % curing (filled circle) and cured (square), as medians over the species' sites. The thin line above each species spans the middle half of its sites' curing dates.",
  "Horizontal timeline per grass species from green-up through 50 % curing to cured, cool-season species in blue at the top and warm-season in orange below.")
```

- **A few species carry the record.** 70 species are observed (29 perennial and 4 annual
  cool-season, 36 perennial and 1 annual warm-season; 12 introduced). The five largest
  (pineland threeawn, blue grama, little bluestem, Kentucky bluegrass and smooth brome) hold
  44 % of the plant-years, and 31 species are seen at a single site.
- **Widespread species give the best view of place.** Little bluestem (23 sites), blue grama and
  sideoats grama (18 each), buffelgrass (15) and switchgrass (14) span several ecoregions; the
  middle half of their sites' curing dates spans six weeks to two and a half months.
- **Most warm-season species cure in September or early October.** Bush muhly in the Warm
  Deserts is earliest among those with three or more sites (end of August) and pineland threeawn, on the Southeastern
  coastal plains, holds 50 % green into December. Among cool-season species the annual
  cheatgrass cures in mid-May, four months before the perennials.
- Grass type (C3 / C4), life cycle and origin are assigned by species from the literature, to be
  reviewed with USA-NPN.

```{r fig-npn-species-sites}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_species_sites",
  "The same species at different sites, for the five species observed at the most sites. Top: typical green-up against the site's March–April mean temperature. Bottom: typical 50 % curing against site aridity (precipitation / potential evapotranspiration). One point per site; point size = years observed.",
  "Ten scatter plots, two rows of five species: green-up dates fall with warmer spring temperature in every species; curing dates show little relation to site wetness except in blue grama.")
```

- **Within a species, green-up follows spring warmth.** Little bluestem, sideoats grama, blue
  grama and big bluestem all green up earlier at warmer sites (rank correlations −0.46 to −0.89),
  so the across-site result above is not just a matter of which species grow where.
- **Curing hardly follows site wetness, even within a species.** Only blue grama cures clearly
  later at wetter sites (r = 0.54, 13 sites); for the others the correlation is between −0.15 and
  0.26. A few sites with early typical curing (for example little bluestem in May–June) are sites
  where the species cures after a spring flush.

```{r fig-npn-species-spread}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_species_spread",
  "How much each species' dates move from year to year (filled) against how much plants of that species differ in the same site and year (open), in the year-to-year set (≥ 12 readings, series with ≥ 3 years); species with at least 10 series-years, ordered by the year-to-year spread of 50 % curing.",
  "Three dot charts, green-up, curing and cured, with one row per species showing the between-year and between-plant standard deviations.")
```

- **Plants differ about as much as years do.** For 50 % curing the year-to-year standard deviation
  is 12–40 days by species (median 26) and the spread between plants in the same site and year is
  about the same (median 24). So a single plant's curing date says little about the year.
- **Some species are steadier.** Big bluestem and Nepalese browntop move about two weeks from year
  to year; blue grama, purple threeawn, Kentucky bluegrass and pineland threeawn move four to six
  weeks, and purple threeawn's plants differ even more than its years. For ground monitoring of curing, the steadier species
  give a clearer year signal per plant observed.

### The species as fuels

U.S. fire danger and fire behavior systems describe grass fuels by fuel bed (load, depth,
climate), not by species, and the one species trait they use is the life cycle: annual grass
cures fully and stays cured. The record can still be read against three fuel attributes: the
life cycle, the invasive grasses known to change fire regimes, and the fuel model at each site.

```{r fig-npn-fuelmodels}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_fuelmodels",
  "Scott & Burgan (2005) fire behavior fuel models (LANDFIRE FBFM40) at the study sites. Left: sites per fuel model (dark: NEON) with their plant-years. Right: typical 50 % curing of each site and species, by fuel model and grass type.",
  "Bar chart of sites per fuel model and a dot plot of typical curing dates by fuel model, cool-season in blue and warm-season in orange.")
```

- **The record is mostly low-load grass fuel.** 40 of the 130 sites sit in a grass fuel model
  (GR), with 73 % of the plant-years; GR2 (low-load, dry-climate grass) alone has 21 sites and half
  of all plant-years, and GR1–GR3 hold nearly all the rest. The tall, heavy grass models (GR5–GR8)
  have 5 sites and 29 plant-years, so the record says little about tallgrass-type fuel beds. Grass-
  shrub (GS, 20 sites), timber litter (TL, 24, grasses in forest understory), shrub (SH,
  11) and timber-understory (TU, 4) make up most of the rest.
- **31 sites are nonburnable at 30 m**, all of them volunteer or managed sites in towns, with 84
  plant-years: their grasses are in yards, campuses and parks rather than in a wildland fuel bed.
- **Curing does not sort by fuel model.** Warm-season grasses at grass-model sites reach 50 %
  curing in late September, as they do at most other sites; cool-season grasses cure earliest at
  shrub and grass-shrub sites (late June and late July) and latest under forest (mid-October). The fuel model describes the fuel bed, while the curing date follows
  the grass type and the place.
- **Mature height and growth form** come from USDA PLANTS for 42 of the 70 species; PLANTS has no
  characteristics for the rest, including cheatgrass and Nepalese browntop.
- **Three invaders that raise fire occurrence are in the record** (marked † in the figures, "yes"
  in the table): cheatgrass (4 sites), buffelgrass (15 sites) and Nepalese browntop (3 sites, 279
  plant-years). Their seasons differ: cheatgrass is fully cured by the end of May, buffelgrass
  reaches 50 % curing in late September with the end of the monsoon, and Nepalese browntop in
  mid-October. So their added fire risk falls in different parts of the year.
- **Annual grasses cure early and completely.** All four annual cool-season grasses (cheatgrass,
  ripgut and soft brome, sixweeks fescue) are cured by mid-June, months before the perennial
  cool-season grasses (see the season by species above). That early, complete curing is why fire
  danger systems treat annual herbaceous fuel separately.

```{r tbl-npn-species}
#| results: asis
sp_f <- "tables/npn_species.csv"
if (file.exists(sp_f)) {
  S <- utils::read.csv(sp_f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  dl <- function(d) ifelse(is.na(d), "", format(as.Date("2001-01-01") + round(d) - 1, "%b %-d"))
  dn <- function(d, n) ifelse(is.na(d), "", sprintf("%s (%d)", dl(d), n))
  pw <- c(C3 = "cool (C3)", C4 = "warm (C4)")
  T <- data.frame(
    Species = sprintf("*%s %s*", S$genus, S$species), `Common name` = S$common_name,
    Type = unname(pw[S$pathway]), `Life cycle` = S$life_cycle, Origin = S$origin,
    `Sites (NEON)` = sprintf("%d (%d)", S$sites, S$sites_neon),
    `Plant-years` = format(S$plant_years, big.mark = ","), Plants = S$plants,
    Readings = format(S$readings, big.mark = ","),
    Years = ifelse(S$first_year == S$last_year, S$first_year, sprintf("%d–%d", S$first_year, S$last_year)),
    `Ecoregions (Level II)` = S$ecoregions, States = S$states,
    `Fire-promoting invader` = ifelse(S$fire_invader %in% "yes", "yes", ""),
    `Mature height (ft)` = ifelse(is.na(S$height_ft), "", format(S$height_ft)),
    `Growth form` = ifelse(is.na(S$growth_form), "", S$growth_form),
    `Fuel models at sites` = ifelse(is.na(S$fuel_models), "", S$fuel_models),
    `Green-up` = dn(S$greenup_doy, S$greenup_series), `50 % curing` = dn(S$curing_doy, S$curing_series),
    Cured = dn(S$cured_doy, S$cured_series), `Year-to-year series` = S$series_yty,
    check.names = FALSE)
  cat('\n::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}\n')
  cat(sprintf("## All %d species: where, how much record, typical dates (click to open)\n\n", nrow(T)))
  cat("Sorted by grass type, then plant-years. Typical dates are circular medians over the species' site series, with the number of series in brackets. Ecoregion codes as in the dates figure. Year-to-year series: site series in the stricter set (≥ 12 readings, ≥ 3 years). Fire-promoting invader: raises fire occurrence and frequency across U.S. ecoregions (Fusco et al. 2019). Height and growth form: USDA PLANTS. Fuel models: Scott & Burgan (2005) model from LANDFIRE at the species' sites (number of sites).\n\n")
  cat("::: {.species-table}\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", rep("r", 5), "l", "l", "l", "r", "l", "l", rep("r", 4))))
  cat("\n\n: Species in the NPN grass percent-green record (relaxed set) {.striped}\n\n:::\n\n:::\n\n")
} else cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Table pending\nRun npn_study/scripts/58c_npn_species.R.\n:::\n\n')
```

### How the record covers U.S. grass fuels

Ground records come from where observers are, not from a design. To see how far the results
reach, the record is set against where grass fuels are in the contiguous U.S.: the LANDFIRE fuel
model map (FBFM40, 30 m), sampled on a regular grid of about 2 million cells, with the cells in a
grass (GR1–GR9) or grass-shrub (GS1–GS4) fuel model taken as grass fuel. Each sampled cell is
given its EPA Level II ecoregion, and each ecoregion's share of U.S. grass fuel area is compared
with its share of the record's sites and plant-years. A coverage ratio near 1 means the record
holds about as much of a region as its grass fuels would claim; well below 1 means
under-sampled.

```{r fig-npn-repr}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_repr",
  "Left: a sample of LANDFIRE grass (GR) and grass-shrub (GS) fuel cells, with the study sites sized by plant-years. Right: each Level II ecoregion's share of U.S. grass fuel area (gray bar), of the record's plant-years (orange bar) and of its sites (blue point).",
  "Map of grass fuel cells and study sites, and a bar chart comparing each ecoregion's share of grass fuel area with its share of the record.")
```

```{r repr-bullets}
#| results: asis
re_f <- "tables/npn_representativeness_ecoregion.csv"; rf_f <- "tables/npn_representativeness_fuelmodel.csv"
if (file.exists(re_f) && file.exists(rf_f)) {
  RE <- utils::read.csv(re_f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(region = "character"))
  RF <- utils::read.csv(rf_f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * x)
  lab <- function(d) paste0(d$name, " (", d$region, ")")
  big <- RE[RE$grass_fuel_area_share >= 0.02, ]
  top <- big[order(-big$grass_fuel_area_share), ][1:min(5, nrow(big)), ]
  under <- big[big$coverage_plant_years < 0.25, ]; under <- under[order(-under$grass_fuel_area_share), ]
  over <- RE[RE$coverage_plant_years >= 2 & RE$plant_year_share >= 0.05, ]; over <- over[order(-over$plant_year_share), ]
  gr <- RF[substr(RF$fuel_model, 1, 2) == "GR", ]; gsx <- RF[substr(RF$fuel_model, 1, 2) == "GS", ]
  heavy <- RF[RF$fuel_model %in% paste0("GR", 4:9), ]
  cat(sprintf("- **Where the grass fuel is.** The five ecoregions with the most grass fuel area hold %s of it: %s. Grass-shrub models make up %s of the grass fuel area and grass models %s.\n",
              pc(sum(top$grass_fuel_area_share)), paste(sprintf("%s %s", lab(top), pc(top$grass_fuel_area_share)), collapse = "; "),
              pc(sum(gsx$grass_fuel_area_share)), pc(sum(gr$grass_fuel_area_share))))
  cat(sprintf("- **Under-sampled.** %d of the %d ecoregions with at least 2 %% of U.S. grass fuel have less than a quarter of their share in plant-years%s.\n",
              nrow(under), nrow(big), if (nrow(under)) paste0(", together ", pc(sum(under$grass_fuel_area_share)), " of the grass fuel area: ",
              paste(sprintf("%s (%s of grass fuel, %s of plant-years, %d %s)", lab(under), pc(under$grass_fuel_area_share), pc(under$plant_year_share), under$sites, ifelse(under$sites == 1, "site", "sites")), collapse = "; ")) else ""))
  if (nrow(over)) cat(sprintf("- **Over-sampled.** %s together hold %s of the plant-years.\n",
              paste(sprintf("%s (%s of plant-years against %s of grass fuel)", lab(over), pc(over$plant_year_share), pc(over$grass_fuel_area_share)), collapse = "; "), pc(sum(over$plant_year_share))))
  cat(sprintf("- **By fuel model.** The tall and heavy grass models GR4–GR9 cover %s of the grass fuel area and hold %s of the plant-years at grass-model sites; grass-shrub models cover %s and hold %s.\n\n",
              pc(sum(heavy$grass_fuel_area_share)), pc(sum(heavy$plant_year_share)), pc(sum(gsx$grass_fuel_area_share)), pc(sum(gsx$plant_year_share))))
  T <- data.frame(Ecoregion = lab(RE), `Grass fuel area` = pc(RE$grass_fuel_area_share), `Sites (NEON)` = sprintf("%d (%d)", RE$sites, RE$sites_neon),
                  `Plant-years` = format(RE$plant_years, big.mark = ","), `Share of plant-years` = pc(RE$plant_year_share),
                  Coverage = sprintf("%.2f", RE$coverage_plant_years), check.names = FALSE)
  T <- T[RE$grass_fuel_area_share > 0 | RE$plant_years > 0, ]
  cat('::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}\n## Coverage by ecoregion and fuel model (click to open)\n\n')
  cat("Grass fuel area: share of sampled LANDFIRE cells in a GR or GS fuel model. Coverage: share of plant-years divided by share of grass fuel area.\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", 5))))
  cat("\n\n: The record against U.S. grass fuel area, by EPA Level II ecoregion {.striped}\n\n")
  U <- data.frame(`Fuel model` = RF$fuel_model, `Grass fuel area` = pc(RF$grass_fuel_area_share), Sites = RF$sites,
                  `Plant-years` = format(RF$plant_years, big.mark = ","), `Share of plant-years at grass-model sites` = pc(RF$plant_year_share), check.names = FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(U, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", 4))))
  cat("\n\n: The record against U.S. grass fuel area, by Scott & Burgan grass and grass-shrub fuel model {.striped}\n\n:::\n\n")
} else cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Results pending\nRun npn_study/scripts/59c_npn_representativeness.R.\n:::\n\n')
```

## When grasses green up and cure

```{r fig-npn-dates}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_dates",
  "Typical green-up, 50 % curing and cured dates by EPA Level II ecoregion and grass type. Each point is one site and species (its typical date over all years observed); the bar is the region median where it has three or more.",
  "Three panels of dot plots: green-up, curing and cured dates by ecoregion, cool-season grasses in blue and warm-season in orange.")
```

```{r fig-npn-region-dates}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_region_dates",
  "The same typical dates as maps: the ecoregion mean of site-and-species typical green-up and 50 % curing dates for cool-season (top) and warm-season (bottom) grasses, where an ecoregion has three or more site series; gray where it has fewer. Dots are the sites observing that grass type. Each panel has its own colour scale.",
  "Four maps of the contiguous U.S. with Level II ecoregions coloured by typical green-up and curing date for cool- and warm-season grasses.")
```

```{r fig-npn-region-c3c4}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_region_c3c4",
  "Warm-season (C4) minus cool-season (C3) typical green-up and 50 % curing date in each ecoregion where both grass types have three or more site series (red: warm-season later; blue: earlier). Purple points are sites observing both types.",
  "Two maps of ecoregions coloured by the difference in typical date between warm- and cool-season grasses, for green-up and curing.")
```

- **The season moves with ecoregion and grass type.** Warm-season grasses on the Mississippi
  Alluvial and Southeast USA Coastal Plains (8.5) green up in late February and cure around
  October 20; in the Warm Deserts (10.2) they green up with the summer rains in late June and cure
  at the end of September. Cool-season grasses cure in mid-May in Mediterranean California
  (11.1), late June in the Cold Deserts (10.1) and late July in the Western Cordillera (6.2),
  and from early August (South Central Semiarid Prairies, 9.4) to late September (West-Central
  Semiarid Prairies, 9.3) on the Great Plains.
- **Cool- versus warm-season depends on the region.** Where both are observed in three or
  more series each, warm-season grasses cure 38 days later than cool-season ones in the South
  Central Semiarid Prairies (9.4) and 75 days later in the Cold Deserts (10.1); on the
  Southeastern USA Plains (8.3) cool-season grasses green up 75 days earlier and cure 29 days
  later. In the Mixed Wood Plains (8.1) and West-Central Semiarid Prairies (9.3) the two types
  differ by less than three weeks.
- **No gap between the cool- and warm-season pulses.** At sites with both types, warm-season
  grasses reach 50 % green four to five months before the cool-season grasses beside them have
  cured: on the Great Plains prairies (Temperate, West-Central and South Central Semiarid
  Prairies, 9.2–9.4) warm-season green-up comes in April to June and cool-season cured dates in
  late September to November, 140–160 days apart. Every year at every such site the two overlap;
  the ground shows no stretch in which neither type is green.
- **Annual grasses cure early.** In the Cold Deserts annual grasses (mostly cheatgrass) cure
  77 days earlier than perennial cool-season grasses, and in the Western Cordillera 97 days
  earlier (3 annual series each).
- **Small cells need care.** Many ecoregion and grass-type combinations rest on 2–5 sites;
  cool-season green-up in early August in the Western Cordillera (three series) reflects
  mountain sites, and single points in other cells may be fall green-ups.

## Do typical dates follow site climate?

Each site and species' typical date was modelled on the site's climate normals (PRISM,
2002–2025), with a random effect for species, and compared with a model of species alone,
one with the ecoregion instead of climate, and one with both. Climate is a small set
chosen in advance: March–April mean temperature for green-up, July–August mean temperature
for curing, and for both aridity (precipitation / potential evapotranspiration), the share
of rain falling July–September and latitude. Each model is scored by refitting it with one
site left out at a time and predicting that site. Many NPN sites are plots a few kilometres apart
(41 of the 130 have another site within 2 km), so the models are also scored by leaving out whole
clusters of sites within 10 km and within 50 km of each other: a fairer test of predicting a new
place.

| Date | Grass type | Series (sites) | Species only | Ecoregion | Site climate | Ecoregion + climate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | warm-season (C4) | 115 (66) | 0.39 | 0.40 | **0.61** | 0.59 |
| Green-up | cool-season (C3) | 36 (25) | −0.23 | 0.15 | 0.19 | below −1 |
| 50 % curing | warm-season (C4) | 123 (61) | 0.02 | −0.10 | 0.00 | −0.13 |
| 50 % curing | cool-season (C3) | 62 (38) | **0.63** | 0.59 | **0.63** | 0.04 |
| Cured | warm-season (C4) | 110 (56) | −0.10 | −0.10 | −0.01 | −0.17 |
| Cured | cool-season (C3) | 58 (34) | **0.65** | 0.59 | 0.64 | 0.04 |

: Share of the variation in typical dates predicted at a site left out (R², 0 = no better than the mean) {.striped}

| Date | Grass type | Model | One site out | Sites within 10 km out | Within 50 km out |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | warm-season (C4) | species only | 0.39 | 0.09 | −0.08 |
| | | ecoregion | 0.40 | 0.23 | 0.29 |
| | | site climate | 0.61 | **0.30** | 0.20 |
| | | ecoregion + climate | 0.59 | **0.39** | 0.29 |
| 50 % curing | cool-season (C3) | species only | 0.63 | 0.62 | 0.36 |
| | | site climate | 0.63 | **0.61** | **0.48** |
| Cured | cool-season (C3) | species only | 0.65 | 0.63 | 0.30 |
| | | site climate | 0.64 | **0.60** | **0.42** |

: The same models scored by leaving out clusters of nearby sites (R²; from npn_study/scripts/58e_npn_spatial_cv.R) {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-spatial}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_spatial",
  "Typical dates against site climate. Left: how well each model (species only, ecoregion, site climate, both) predicts a left-out site. Middle: typical green-up against March–April temperature. Right: typical 50 % curing against site aridity.",
  "Three panels: dot chart of leave-one-site-out R-squared for four models, three dates and three grass groups; scatter of green-up date against spring temperature; scatter of curing date against aridity.")
```

- **Warm-season green-up follows site climate,** about 38 days earlier per standard deviation
  of warmer March–April temperature, and 27 days later per standard deviation more of the rain
  in summer (the monsoon sites green up with the summer rains).
- **But nearby plots inflate the one-site-out score.** Holding out sites within 10 km together,
  site climate predicts 30 % of the variation in warm-season typical green-up at a new place
  (61 % with one site out), and ecoregion plus climate 39 %; within 50 km climate falls to 20 %
  and the ecoregion does about as well (29 %). Species alone falls to almost nothing: a species'
  typical date at one plot was mostly being learned from the plot next to it. In the stricter
  year-to-year set the climate model holds up better (0.54, 0.49, 0.57).
- **Cool-season curing holds up best.** Site climate still predicts 61 % of the variation in
  typical 50 % curing with sites within 10 km held out, and 48 % within 50 km.
- **Cool-season green-up tracks spring temperature too** (rank correlation about −0.8 to
  −0.9 depending on the series included), but with 25 sites the models do not hold up at a
  left-out site.
- **Cool-season curing and the cured date follow the species about as well as the climate.**
  Wetter sites, and sites with more summer rain, cure 20–25 days later per standard
  deviation; but which species grow where already carries most of that.
- **Warm-season curing and cured dates are not explained across sites** by species, region
  or climate.
- **Adding the ecoregion to the climate overfits for cool-season grasses** (25–38 sites); for
  warm-season green-up it helps once nearby plots are held out.
- The same holds, more weakly, in the stricter year-to-year set.

## Can weather beat the typical date?

| Date | Series-years | Typical-date error | L1 | L2 | L3 | L4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 289 | 24.8 days | 0.00 | −0.04 | −0.02 | −0.02 |
| 50 % curing | 529 | 27.6 days | 0.00 | −0.33 | −0.04 | −0.02 |
| Cured | 461 | 23.7 days | +0.01 | −0.17 | −0.05 | −0.03 |

: Skill against the typical date (0 = no better, negative = worse), lead driver set {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-ladder}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_ladder",
  "Skill of each model against the typical date (0 = no better, negative = worse), lead driver set, leave-one-year-out. Black: all grasses; blue: cool-season; orange: warm-season.",
  "Dot charts of skill for four model levels and three dates; all points sit at or below zero.")
```

- **No step beats the typical date.** The best is one driver for the cured date (+0.01,
  correlation 0.15). The process rules, the regression and the random forest all add
  error. The same holds for C3 and C4 separately, in each region with enough data, when
  species are averaged within a site-year, and with the hindcast drivers that can see
  past the date.
- **The same limit shows up in fire prediction.** A related fire study found that curing
  forecast from weather 14 days ahead (refit for every region, leaving one year out) added nothing
  to predicting fire activity, while satellite-observed curing did.
- **The regression does not settle on drivers.** Its choices change from one left-out
  year to the next.
- **The ceiling is low.** Species observed at the same site in the same year share only
  part of their early or late year: 22 % of the year-to-year variance for green-up, 24 %
  for curing and 40 % for the cured date. The rest is specific to the plant or the
  observer, which no weather record can explain.

## How much of the year-to-year variation could weather explain?

To measure the ceiling directly, each plant's date is split into parts with a mixed model
on all plant-years (5,780 plant-years, 1,514 plants, 84 sites; plant dates more than 90 days
from the series' usual date, 5–10 %, are left out): place (site, species, and
the species at that site), a year signal shared by the grasses at a site (national,
regional and site-wide), a year signal of one species at one site, and what is left for
the single plant.

| Date | Plant-years | Place, % of all variation | Year-to-year SD | Shared by the site's grasses | Region-wide part of that | One species only | Single plant |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 2,563 | 70 % | 30 days | 37 % | 12 % | 24 % | 40 % |
| 50 % curing | 4,468 | 71 % | 36 days | 28 % | 14 % | 20 % | 52 % |
| Cured | 3,225 | 80 % | 30 days | 39 % | 8 % | 22 % | 39 % |

: Variance partition of NPN grass dates; the last four columns are shares of the year-to-year variation {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-variance}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_variance",
  "What the year-to-year variation in each date is made of: shared across the region, shared by the grasses at a site, specific to one species at a site, or specific to the single plant.",
  "Stacked horizontal bars of the four shares for green-up, curing and cured, all grasses and by grass type.")
```

- **Place dominates.** 70–80 % of the variation in a plant's date is where
  it grows and what species it is. That is what the typical-date maps carry.
- **Of the year-to-year part, 28–39 % is shared** by the grasses at a site:
  about 18 days (standard deviation) for each date. That shared part is the most any
  weather record at the site could explain, and the ladder above explained almost none of
  it. So the ceiling is real but not zero: the weather drivers tried so far miss a
  shared signal that exists.
- **Little of it is region-wide.** Within an ecoregion, the part every site shares is 12 %
  of green-up's year-to-year variation, 14 % of curing's and 8 % of the cured date's; most of
  the shared signal is local to the site. Local weather is one explanation; so are things that
  act on a whole site in a year, such as mowing, grazing, irrigation or a change of observer,
  which the data cannot separate.
- **Half of the year-to-year variation in 50 % curing belongs to the single plant**,
  more for warm-season (C4) grasses (62 %) than cool-season (C3, 37 %). The spacing of
  readings accounts for only 1–3 % of it, so it is not a sampling artefact: plants of one
  species at one site really differ (microsite, age, how each observer judges "percent
  green").
- **Averaging the plants helps but does not remove it.** In a site-species-year mean
  (median 3–5 plants) the shared part is about half (48–55 %) of the year-to-year variation.
- **A satellite check points the same way.** In a related fire study, early or late curing in a
  4 km satellite record agreed with NPN departures at r = 0.35 for single site-years, but at
  r = 0.66 once both were averaged over a region's sites in a year (72 region-years; 0.74–0.84 on
  the Great Plains, southern Plains and in the monsoon Southwest, 0.20 in the upper Midwest), as
  expected if much of the scatter at a site is plant-to-plant noise rather than missed weather.

### The partition region by region

The same model fitted within each ecoregion (green-up and curing, all grasses; where a region
has at least 60 plant-years and 4 years) shows whether the small region-wide share is the same
everywhere or is concentrated in a few places.

```{r fig-npn-region-variance}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_region_variance",
  "Top: the share of year-to-year variation shared across each ecoregion (the year term of a model fitted within that region), with the year-to-year standard deviation; gray where the region has too little record to fit. Bottom: the full split by region, ordered by the region-wide share.",
  "Two maps of ecoregions coloured by the region-wide share of year-to-year variation for green-up and curing, and two stacked bar charts of the variance shares by ecoregion.")
```

```{r region-variance-bullets}
#| results: asis
vr_f <- "tables/npn_variance_region.csv"
if (file.exists(vr_f)) {
  V <- utils::read.csv(vr_f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(region = "character"))
  rn <- if (file.exists("../data/npn_site_ecoregions.csv")) { e <- unique(utils::read.csv("../data/npn_site_ecoregions.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(eco_l2_code = "character"))[, c("eco_l2_code", "eco_l2_name")])
    stats::setNames(gsub("\\bUsa\\b", "USA", tools::toTitleCase(tolower(e$eco_l2_name))), e$eco_l2_code) } else character()
  lab <- function(k) ifelse(k %in% names(rn), paste0(rn[k], " (", k, ")"), k)
  pc <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * x)
  for (tg in c("curing", "greenup")) {
    d <- V[V$target == tg & !V$one_site, ]; if (!nrow(d)) next
    d <- d[order(-d$share_region_year), ]
    hi <- d[d$share_region_year >= 0.25, ]; lo <- d[d$share_region_year < 0.10, ]
    cat(sprintf("- **%s.** Fitted in %d ecoregions with more than one site. The region-wide share ranges from %s to %s (median %s). %s%s The year-to-year standard deviation runs from %.0f days (%s) to %.0f days (%s).\n",
      c(curing = "50 % curing", greenup = "Green-up")[[tg]], nrow(d), pc(min(d$share_region_year)), pc(max(d$share_region_year)), pc(stats::median(d$share_region_year)),
      if (nrow(hi)) paste0("A quarter or more is region-wide only in ", paste(sprintf("%s, %s", lab(hi$region), pc(hi$share_region_year)), collapse = "; "), ". ") else "No region has a quarter or more region-wide. ",
      if (nrow(lo)) sprintf("In %d of them it is under 10 %%.", nrow(lo)) else "",
      min(d$sd_year_to_year), lab(d$region[which.min(d$sd_year_to_year)]), max(d$sd_year_to_year), lab(d$region[which.max(d$sd_year_to_year)])))
  }
  one <- V[V$one_site, ]
  if (nrow(one)) cat(sprintf("- **One-site regions** (%s) are shown, but there the year term is that one site's year signal, not a regional one.\n", paste(unique(lab(one$region)), collapse = ", ")))
  cat("- **So a regional weather signal is the exception.** Where the record is deep enough to fit, most regions share little of a year's departure across their sites; the shared part sits at the site, the species or the plant.\n\n")
} else cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Results pending\nRun npn_study/scripts/53b_npn_variance_region.R.\n:::\n\n')
```

## Does the shared signal follow local weather?

The shared part was estimated for each
site-year from the same model (203–290 site-years at 64–71 sites) and compared with that
year's weather departures at the site.

- **For curing and the cured date it does, weakly, and in the expected direction.** Sites with
  more summer rain events or lower summer vapour pressure deficit cure later (correlations
  about 0.15–0.25; strongest: June–August VPD, April–September rain events, and VPD in the 30
  days before the typical date).
- **But not enough to predict it.** Fitted on the other years, a selected set of drivers
  explains none of the shared signal in a left-out year. So most of the site-wide year signal is something the 4 km weather record
  does not see: very local weather and soil, or what happens at the site (mowing, grazing,
  irrigation, a new observer).
```{r fig-npn-signal}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_signal",
  "The shared site-year signal against June–August vapour pressure deficit, both as departures within each year: higher summer VPD goes with earlier curing, but the scatter is wide.",
  "Two scatter plots with a downward-sloping fitted line, curing and cured.")
```

- **Managed sites are not the explanation.** Gardens, yards, campuses and parks are only
  about 4 % of the usable plant-years, too few to fit on their own; the results without them
  are unchanged.
- **The year-to-year record is mostly NEON.** 96 % of the plant-years in this set come from
  the 36 National Ecological Observatory Network field sites, where trained technicians
  follow five tagged plants per species in natural plots. Results without NEON sites are too
  thin to compare (124–154 plant-years). So the large plant share is not volunteer noise: it is real
  plant-to-plant variation within a plot plus how each technician judges "percent green",
  and the site-wide year signal may include crew changes and visit schedules as well as
  weather.
- **For green-up, the links are with summer temperature, after the event,** so they reflect
  which years were warm overall rather than a cause, and they do not carry over to a
  left-out year either.

## A check: 2016 and 2017

In most years about 1 % of NEON plant-years never pass 50 % green. In 2016 it was 16 % and
in 2017 30 %, at 11 of the 18 NEON sites observed then; in those two years only 53 % of
plant-years reached the top class (95 % green or more), against 89 % in other years. A
change that shows up at most sites at once, in two consecutive years, points to how
percent green was judged rather than to weather. A plant that peaks lower crosses 50 % on
the way down earlier, so those years could look like early-curing years everywhere.

```{r fig-npn-sensitivity}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_sensitivity",
  "Left: share of NEON plant-years that never pass 50 % green, by year. Right: the share of the year-to-year variation shared by a site's grasses, with all years and without 2016–2017.",
  "Bar chart by year with 2016 and 2017 standing out; paired bars for green-up, curing and cured.")
```

| | All years | Without 2016–17 |
|---|---|---|
| Best model skill against the typical date: green-up / curing / cured | 0.00 / 0.00 / +0.01 | +0.02 / 0.00 / +0.01 |
| Shared by the site's grasses (% of year-to-year): green-up | 37 % | 28 % |
| — 50 % curing | 28 % | 20 % |
| — cured | 39 % | 38 % |
| Region-wide part: green-up / curing / cured | 12 / 14 / 8 % | 15 / 6 / 10 % |

: The year-to-year results with and without 2016–2017 (series-years and plant-years in those years dropped) {.striped}

- **The conclusions do not change.** Nothing beats the typical date either way.
- **But more than a quarter of the shared curing signal was 2016–17.** Without them, the year
  signal shared by a site's grasses is 20 % of the year-to-year variation in 50 % curing rather
  than 28 %; the cured date is unaffected, as expected if those years mostly lowered the
  peak.
- **Without them, curing follows moisture more clearly.** Wetter years cure later, with
  correlations of about 0.22 for annual rain, April–September rain events and the 60-day
  moisture memory (23 of 61 drivers significant, against 2 with all years), yet still too
  weakly to predict a left-out year.
- The main results keep all years; this check is reported alongside until USA-NPN and NEON
  can say whether guidance or training for percent green changed around 2018.

## Robustness of the curve dates

Every result above rests on the 50 % crossings of each plant's percent-green curve. To check how
much they depend on that choice, green-up and 50 % curing were recomputed for every usable
plant-year from the readings, at 40 % and 60 % instead of 50 %, with a limit of 21 or 14 days on
the gap between the two readings around the crossing, and with curing taken on the first fall
below 50 % after green-up rather than the fall after the season's peak. Each version went through
the same typical dates, variance partition and single-driver weather test as the main results.

```{r tbl-npn-date-sens}
#| results: asis
sf <- "tables/npn_date_sensitivity.csv"
if (file.exists(sf)) {
  S <- utils::read.csv(sf, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  vl <- c(reference = "As used (02c)", own50 = "Recomputed, 50 %", th40 = "40 % green", th60 = "60 % green", gap21 = "Readings <= 21 d apart",
          gap14 = "Readings <= 14 d apart", firstcycle = "Curing on the first cycle")
  pc <- function(z) ifelse(is.na(z), "", sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * z))
  T <- data.frame(Version = vl[S$variant], Date = c(greenup = "green-up", curing = "curing")[S$target], `Plant-years` = format(S$plant_years, big.mark = ","),
                  `Median change (days)` = sprintf("%.1f", S$median_abs_diff), `Typical date shift (days)` = sprintf("%+.1f", S$typical_shift_median),
                  `Place, % of all` = pc(S$place_share), `Shared, % of year-to-year` = pc(S$shared_share), `Single plant, % of year-to-year` = pc(S$plant_share),
                  `Weather skill` = sprintf("%+.2f", S$weather_skill), check.names = FALSE)
  T <- T[order(T$Date, match(S$variant, names(vl))), ]
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", 7))))
  cat("\n\n: The main results with the curve dates computed in other ways (from npn_study/scripts/58f_npn_date_sensitivity.R) {.striped}\n\n")
}
```

- **The threshold barely matters.** Taking 40 % or 60 % instead of 50 % moves a plant's date by
  about 2 days and the typical dates by about 2 days, with the variance shares and the weather
  result unchanged. NPN's classes explain why: all three thresholds fall between the same two
  classes (25–49 % and 50–74 %), so only the interpolation between the two readings changes.
- **Requiring close readings drops dates but changes no conclusion.** Limiting the gap around the
  crossing to 21 or 14 days removes 10–12 % of the green-ups recomputed without a limit and 5–7 %
  of the curing dates; the shares move by a few points.
- **The curing cycle matters for some plants.** Taking the first fall below 50 % instead of the
  fall after the peak moves the typical curing date of some series by weeks (middle half of
  shifts 12 days) and lowers the shared year signal from 30 % to 23 % of the year-to-year
  variation; nothing beats the typical date either way.
- **The recomputation matches the dates used.** At 50 % with no gap limit, the recomputed dates
  equal those used throughout (median difference 0 days) wherever both exist; the recomputation
  finds more green-ups because the dates used require more of a curve before green-up.

### Uncertainty in the headline numbers

```{r tbl-npn-boot}
#| results: asis
bf <- "tables/npn_bootstrap.csv"
if (file.exists(bf)) {
  Bt <- utils::read.csv(bf, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  lab <- c(variance_place_greenup = "Green-up: place, share of all variation", variance_shared_greenup = "Green-up: shared by a site's grasses, share of year-to-year",
           variance_plant_greenup = "Green-up: single plant, share of year-to-year", weather_skill_greenup = "Green-up: best single lead weather driver, skill",
           variance_place_curing = "50 % curing: place, share of all variation", variance_shared_curing = "50 % curing: shared by a site's grasses, share of year-to-year",
           variance_plant_curing = "50 % curing: single plant, share of year-to-year", weather_skill_curing = "50 % curing: best single lead weather driver, skill",
           variance_place_cured = "Cured: place, share of all variation", variance_shared_cured = "Cured: shared by a site's grasses, share of year-to-year",
           variance_plant_cured = "Cured: single plant, share of year-to-year", weather_skill_cured = "Cured: best single lead weather driver, skill",
           climate_c4_greenup_days_per_sd_t_marapr = "Warm-season green-up: days per SD of March-April temperature",
           c3c4_gap_prairie_days = "Prairies: C4 green-up minus C3 cured, days")
  sh <- grepl("^variance", Bt$statistic); f <- function(z, s) ifelse(s, sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * z), sprintf("%.2f", z))
  f2 <- function(z, s, st) ifelse(s, sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * z), ifelse(grepl("days", st), sprintf("%.0f", z), sprintf("%.2f", z)))
  T <- data.frame(Quantity = lab[Bt$statistic], Estimate = f2(Bt$estimate, sh, Bt$statistic),
                  `95 % interval` = sprintf("%s to %s", f2(Bt$lo, sh, Bt$statistic), f2(Bt$hi, sh, Bt$statistic)), check.names = FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r")))
  cat(sprintf("\n\n: Headline numbers with 95 %% intervals from %d bootstrap resamples of site clusters (sites within 10 km resampled together; from npn_study/scripts/58g_npn_bootstrap.R) {.striped}\n\n", Bt$B[1]))
}
```

- **The weather result is the firmest.** For all three dates the 95 % interval of the best single
  lead driver's skill tops out at +0.02 or below: resampling sites never makes weather beat the
  typical date.
- **The variance shares are less precise than single numbers suggest.** Place is 70–80 % of all
  variation (intervals from about 40 % to 87 %); of the year-to-year part, the share shared by a
  site's grasses is 28–39 % but could be anywhere from about a fifth to two-thirds, and the single
  plant 39–52 % (about a fifth to three-fifths). A handful of NEON sites with many plants carry
  these estimates, so which sites are in the sample matters.
- **The across-space and C3 / C4 results hold.** Warm-season grasses green up 38 days earlier per
  standard deviation of warmer March–April temperature (19 to 65 days); on the prairie ecoregions
  warm-season grasses reach 50 % green about 150 days before the cool-season grasses beside them
  have cured (147 to 198 days), never close to a gap.

## Independent checks with LTER records

Two Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) sites in New Mexico have kept their own monthly grass
phenology records, with their own protocols and observers, for decades: the **Jornada** Basin LTER
(15 net primary production sites in five vegetation zones, 1992–2021; each month every plant of
the monitored species is tallied as dormant, non-reproductive, in bud, flowering or fruiting) and
the **Sevilleta** LTER (core sites in black grama and blue grama grassland and creosote shrubland,
2000–2025; each month the first 10 plants of each species on four transects are scored as new
green leaves, old green leaves, brown or leafless). Both give the **share of plants that are
green** each month, not the percent green of a plant; 50 % dates below are where that share
crosses one half. Jornada monitors 21 grasses, all warm-season; Sevilleta 51 (9 cool-season).

```{r fig-npn-lter-c3c4}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_lter_c3c4",
  "Monthly share of grass plants with new green leaves (left) and any green leaves (middle) at Sevilleta, cool-season (C3) and warm-season (C4) grasses pooled over the core sites; right, warm-season grasses at Jornada by vegetation zone. Lines are medians over years, bands the middle half of years.",
  "Three line charts by month: at Sevilleta the cool-season share with new leaves dips in June and July while the warm-season share stays high; at Jornada warm-season grasses are green from April to November in every zone.")
```

- **In the desert, cool- and warm-season grasses also overlap.** At Sevilleta warm-season grasses
  are already putting on new leaves in March (87 % of plants), so the two types grow together
  through spring. In early summer the cool-season grasses slow: the share with new leaves falls
  from about 80 % in May to 54 % in June and 42 % in July and recovers after the monsoon. Both
  types are below half with new leaves in July in a quarter of site-years and in late autumn; a
  regular dry gap between the two pulses does not appear, as on the Plains. The cool-season
  grasses are sparse at these sites (41 months over 11 years with at least 10 plants), so this
  part rests on few years.
- **Green-up in the desert has two modes.** Black grama and bush muhly usually green up in March or
  April; in about a quarter of years they wait for the monsoon and green up in June–August.
- **The two records agree on the seasonal shape.** For the 15 grasses both record, the monthly
  share green at Jornada and Sevilleta tracks the NPN share of readings above 5 % green at NPN
  sites within 400 km (r = 0.87 and 0.81 over species and months).
- **They do not agree on the years.** For black grama at Jornada, the LTER plots and the NEON plots
  agree month by month (r = 0.63, 2015–2021) but not on whether a given month was early or late
  for the time of year (r = 0.11 on the departures). Year-to-year departures at one place depend
  on the plots and observers, as the plant share in the variance partition implies.
- **The 2016–17 low peaks are a NEON feature.** In 2016 and 2017, 15–23 % of NEON series never
  passed 50 % green, against almost none in other years; at Jornada and Sevilleta the share of
  series that never reached half the plants green stayed at 0–3 % in those years. The LTER
  observers saw nothing unusual, which supports a change in how percent green was judged.
- **Under one climate, place matters little.** The same species at the 15 Jornada sites, which
  share one climate, differ by about 10 days in their typical dates (SD across sites), against
  about 56 days from year to year. Nationally place dominates because climate differs; within one
  climate the years dominate.

```{r fig-npn-lter-agree}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_lter_agree",
  "Left: monthly share green for the same species in the LTER records and at NPN sites within 400 km. Middle: black grama at Jornada, LTER plots and NEON plots, same months. Right: share of series that never pass 50 % green, by year (2016–17 shaded).",
  "Scatter of LTER against NPN monthly shares close to the one-to-one line; two monthly time series that rise and fall together; three lines by year where only the NEON line rises in 2016 and 2017.")
```

**Translating between the protocols.** On the NPN record itself (weekly readings at NEON sites),
reading only once a month moves the 50 % dates by about 17 days (green-up later, curing earlier;
10–14 % of dates lost). A population date in the LTER style, "half the plants at least 50 % green",
falls within a few days of the median plant's 50 % green-up and about 19 days after its 50 %
curing; "half the plants with any green", which is what the LTER categories record, comes about a
month earlier in spring and six weeks later in fall. LTER and NPN dates are therefore compared as
seasonal shapes and departures, not as interchangeable dates.

```{r tbl-npn-lter-cal}
#| results: asis
cf <- "tables/lter_calibration.csv"
if (file.exists(cf)) {
  C <- utils::read.csv(cf, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  T <- data.frame(Comparison = C$test, `Plant-years / series` = C$n, `Bias (days)` = sprintf("%+.0f", C$bias), `Mean abs. difference (days)` = sprintf("%.0f", C$mae),
                  `Dates lost` = ifelse(is.na(C$lost), "", sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * C$lost)), check.names = FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")))
  cat("\n\n: Calibration of monthly and population dates on the NPN record {.striped}\n\n")
}
```

```{r fig-npn-lter-weather}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_lter_weather",
  "Year to year at the LTER sites: skill of the best single weather driver against each series' mean (left), and the share of series that green up with the monsoon rather than in spring against December–May rain (right, one point per year).",
  "Dot chart of leave-one-year-out skill by site, grass type and date; scatter of the yearly share of monsoon green-ups against winter-spring rain.")
```

- **Winter–spring rain decides whether desert grasses green up in spring or wait for the
  monsoon.** With daily PRISM at the LTER sites and the same weather drivers as the model ladder,
  the share of warm-season series that first pass half the plants green only after June 1 follows
  December–May rain from year to year: r = −0.77 over 20 years at Jornada (monsoon green-up years
  had 22 mm of December–May rain on average, spring green-up years 78 mm) and r = −0.45 over 24
  years at Sevilleta (34 vs 65 mm).
- **A single site's date stays hard to predict.** For one series in one year, the best single
  driver (chosen within the training years, as the ladder's L1) does a little better than the
  series mean at Jornada (skill +0.13 for green-up, from winter rain, r = −0.60; +0.12 for the
  autumn fall, from autumn rain) and about as well as the mean at Sevilleta (−0.05 to +0.05).
  The weather signal is real but shows up when many series are averaged within a year, as the
  satellite check did when it rose from r = 0.35 at single site-years to 0.66 at the regional
  scale; one plot in one year carries too much plot and observer noise to show it.

**The NPN record at the same scale.** The model ladder scored single series-years. The same
departures and site-year weather were therefore averaged to the site (mean over its species) and
the ecoregion (mean over at least three series at two or more sites) in each year, and the same
single-driver test was repeated at each scale, with the ladder's lead rule (only drivers whose
window ends at least 14 days before the typical date).

```{r fig-npn-scale}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_scale",
  "NPN year-to-year departures at three scales: one series, the site mean and the ecoregion mean in a year. Left: variance of the averaged departures relative to what plant and series noise alone would give (above 1 = a shared year signal). Right: leave-one-year-out skill of the best single lead weather driver.",
  "Two dot charts by date and grass type: the signal ratios at site and ecoregion scale are mostly between 1.5 and 4.5; the skills stay at or below zero at every scale.")
```

- **The shared year signal is there.** Averaged over a site's species or an ecoregion's series, the
  departures vary 1.4–4.5 times more than plant and series noise alone would make them, for all
  three dates, as the variance partition implies.
- **Lead weather still does not predict it, even averaged.** At the ecoregion scale the best single
  lead driver scores −0.34 to +0.06 against no departure (22–48 ecoregion-years per date and grass
  type); at the site scale −0.22 to +0.01. Without 2016–17 the picture is the same. Drivers that
  can see past the date do a little better for green-up (+0.13 to +0.15, from September–October
  temperature), which reflects warm years rather than a cause, as in the ladder.
- **Why the LTER records differ.** Their weather signal is the desert's switch between spring and
  monsoon green-up, decided by winter–spring rain and seen over 20–24 years at one place. The NPN
  record has 11 years, few desert series and few ecoregion-years with several series, so a signal
  of that size could exist and still not be found; what it can say is that no single weather driver
  carries the year signal across U.S. grasslands.

## How much monitoring would it take?

The variance partition says how the year-to-year variation splits between a regional year signal,
the site, the species at the site and the single plant. That is enough to ask what a monitoring
design can measure. For a region with a given number of sites, species per site and plants per
species, the regional mean departure in a year measures the true regional year signal with a known
reliability (the share of its variance that is signal); and if a weather driver explains a given
share of that signal, the number of years needed to detect it follows (two-sided 5 % test, 80 %
power). The driver is assumed to act on the regional signal only; drivers that vary from site to
site could also explain part of the site-year part.

```{r fig-npn-power}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_power",
  "Left and middle: reliability of the regional mean departure in a year, by number of sites and plants per species (two species per site), for 50 % curing and green-up. Right: years of monitoring needed to detect a weather driver that explains half (solid) or a quarter (dashed) of the regional year signal, with two species and five plants per site.",
  "Three line charts: reliability rises steeply with the number of sites and only slightly with plants per species; the years needed fall from about 50-70 with one site to 15-20 with twenty, all above the 11 years of this record.")
```

```{r tbl-npn-power}
#| results: asis
pf <- "tables/npn_power_current.csv"
if (file.exists(pf)) {
  P <- utils::read.csv(pf, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  T <- data.frame(Date = c(greenup = "green-up", curing = "50 % curing", cured = "cured")[P$target], `Sites in the region` = P$n_sites,
                  Design = sprintf("2 species x %d plants", P$n_plants), Reliability = sprintf("%.2f", P$reliability),
                  `Power in 11 years (driver explains half / a quarter)` = sprintf("%.0f %% / %.0f %%", 100 * P$power_11y_half, 100 * P$power_11y_quarter),
                  `Years for 80 % power (half / a quarter)` = sprintf("%d / %d", P$years_80_half, P$years_80_quarter), check.names = FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(T, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r")))
  cat("\n\n: What the record's design can detect (plants per species as in the year-to-year set; from npn_study/scripts/58h_npn_power.R) {.striped}\n\n")
}
```

- **Sites, not plants.** For 50 % curing, going from one to twenty plants per species at a single
  site raises the reliability of a year's mean from 0.22 to 0.35; going from one site to ten
  (five plants per species) raises it from 0.32 to 0.82. The site-year and species-at-site parts
  only average out across sites, and past three to five plants per species extra plants add
  little.
- **The null weather result was to be expected.** With the record's design (one to three sites in
  a region, two species, three to five plants per species) and 11 years, a weather driver that
  explained half of the regional year signal in curing would be detected only 22–40 % of the time;
  for green-up 16–31 %, for the cured date 12–24 %. Detecting it reliably would take about 25–47
  years for curing with that design, or about 17 years with ten sites in the region.
- **For monitoring:** to track year-to-year curing on the ground, spread the effort over more sites
  in a region, with a few plants of the main species at each, read through the end of the season
  for many years; adding plants at existing sites buys little.

## What it means so far

On the ground, the typical date is the baseline to beat, and so far nothing beats it. The typical date itself is
predictable for green-up, which follows site climate, and much less so for curing, which
follows the species for cool-season grasses and nothing measured here for warm-season
ones. There is a shared year signal, mostly local to the site, that
moisture and VPD track only weakly; part of the curing signal looks like a 2016–17 change
in how plants were judged. A first check with the PhenoCam cameras at the NEON plots was
not a fair test: the camera transition dates skip years with a weak green-up, mark a
different stage of the season (the end of the spring flush rather than half-cured plants),
and switch between seasons at sites that green up twice. A comparison based on camera
greenness around each site's typical curing date would avoid those problems; it is on hold.

For fire danger this points three ways. The typical date by place and grass type is the
starting point, and on the Great Plains it has no gap between the cool- and warm-season
pulses: warm-season grasses are green through cool-season curing. Year-to-year departures
are better observed than forecast: weather adds little skill at a single site, while averaged over
a region's sites the ground departures agree with satellite curing (r = 0.66). And single
plants are noisy, so ground monitoring needs several plants and sites to give a regional
signal. A year signal shared by a site's or a region's grasses is there, but in the 11-year NPN
record no single weather driver known beforehand predicts it, even averaged by ecoregion; the longer
LTER records show one case where weather does decide it: in the desert, winter–spring rain sets
whether grasses green up in spring or wait for the monsoon.

## Toward a paper

A draft outline, framed as a data and methods paper. Title idea: *Grass green-up and curing on
the ground: a national record from NEON and USA-NPN percent-green observations*.

**Contribution.** The first national ground record of when U.S. grasses green up and cure, by
ecoregion and grass type; evidence that typical green-up follows site climate while typical
curing largely does not; and evidence that weather adds no skill over the typical date from
year to year, with the reason (most of the year-to-year scatter belongs to single plants).
The typical date is therefore the baseline for grass fuel monitoring, and any weather
adjustment has to beat it on ground data. ("First" still needs a literature check.)

1. **Introduction.** Curing is the grass fuel variable fire managers need and has almost no
   ground record in the U.S.; NPN's percent-green question is, in practice, a curing
   measurement.
2. **Data and methods.** The record and its filters; curve dates; C3 / C4 and life-cycle
   labels; PRISM metrics and normals; ecoregions; typical dates, spatial models, variance
   partition, model ladder.
3. **The record (Q1).** Size and coverage, reading density, use of the percent-green classes,
   second green-ups, plants that never pass 50 %. Figures: site map, record.
4. **Typical dates (Q2).** By ecoregion and grass type; cool- versus warm-season and annual
   versus perennial contrasts; no gap between the cool- and warm-season pulses. Figure: dates by
   ecoregion.
5. **What sets the typical date across sites (Q4).** Green-up follows site climate; cool-season
   curing follows the species; warm-season curing is unexplained. Figure: spatial.
6. **Year to year (Q3, Q5, Q6).** Place dominates; a small shared year signal tracked weakly by
   moisture; no model beats the typical date, simple process rules included. Figures:
   variance, ladder, shared signal.
7. **Data quality: 2016–2017.** What it is and what it changes (pending USA-NPN / NEON).
8. **Discussion.** The typical date as the baseline for fire danger; why prediction from year to
   year is capped; why warm-season curing resists explanation; recommendations for monitoring
   (read through the end of the season, the same plants for several years, several plants per
   species, wildland sites, clearer percent-green guidance).
9. **Conclusions.**

Supplement: filter funnel, the stricter year-to-year set as a sensitivity, the C3 / C4 table,
per-ecoregion tables. Open: venue (*International Journal of Wildland Fire*, *Fire*, a
phenology or data journal), co-authors from USA-NPN, whether to invite NEON, and whether the
PhenoCam comparison earns a place.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 11 2026 | Scope: NPN "percent green" records for grasses with daily PRISM; no GSI, no soil data | Curing measured directly; mapped soil is unlikely to describe the soil under a tagged plant |
| Oct 11 2026 | Moisture as a running P − PET memory (15, 30, 60 days) instead of a soil bucket | Carries wet and dry spells without a soil parameter |
| Oct 15 2026 | A companion study to the regions work, with its own page; code shared with the regions work (superseded Oct 18) | Reuses the PRISM, cue and region code; region numbers match the maps |
| Oct 15 2026 | Cool- and warm-season (C3/C4) assigned by species from the literature, to be reviewed with USA-NPN | No national C3/C4 grass layer |
| Oct 15 2026 | At least 12 readings per plant-year; series need 3 or more years; dates more than 90 days from a series' usual date counted as a season mismatch | Enough readings to place the crossings; mismatches would dominate the errors |
| Oct 15 2026 | Likely managed sites flagged and reported both ways | Gardens and yards may not follow local weather |
| Oct 16 2026 | Normals over 2002–2025 | Daily PRISM used here starts in 2001 |
| Oct 16 2026 | No other plant groups (forbs, shrubs) and no NEON observer or tower-sensor tests | Other groups answer a different percent question; keep the study focused |
| Oct 16 2026 | Two sets: every usable curve (≥ 6 readings, any number of years) for the record, typical dates and climate across space; ≥ 12 readings and ≥ 3 years for the year-to-year analyses | Short volunteer series still give typical dates; year-to-year needs repeated years |
| Oct 16 2026 | NPN-derived "usable" rule (≥ 6 readings, peak above 50 % green) left as is | Sparser volunteer records cannot place a crossing |
| Oct 16 2026 | 2016–2017 reported as a sensitivity check; main results keep all years | Likely a judging change, not yet confirmed with USA-NPN and NEON |
| Oct 18 2026 | A standalone paper, ahead of the fuel phenology regions analysis; its own code folder (`npn_study/`), to become its own repository at publication | The ground record answers its own questions and should not depend on regions built partly from it |
| Oct 18 2026 | EPA Level II ecoregions for all region results | A published regionalization, independent of the fuel phenology regions (which were chosen partly on these ground dates) |
| Oct 16 2026 | Second green-up: below 25 % green, then above 50 % on two readings at least three weeks later | A looser rule mostly caught readings flickering around 50 % |

: Study decisions {.striped}
